title: Centralized custodians and exchanges appear in the Allocation System as governed Instances
content:
Three entries in the Ethereum Mainnet directory are not DeFi protocols at all. A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.1.2.1.12 registers Paxos Instances for USDC→PYUSD, PYUSD→USDC, PYUSD→USDG and USDG→PYUSD conversions. A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.1.2.1.13 registers Anchorage Instances for USAT, USDT and USDC. A.6.1.1.1.2.6.1.1.2.1.14 registers two Binance Instances — "Transfer USDC to Binance (receive USDT)" and the reverse.

The structural claim is that the Allocation System's unit of governance is a **capital route**, not a smart contract. A transfer to a centralized exchange to swap one stablecoin for another is treated exactly like a deposit into a lending pool: it gets a directory entry, an Instance Configuration Document, and the operational process that comes with it.

This matters because the alternative is far worse. Real treasury operations at this size inevitably touch regulated issuers, custodians and exchange liquidity; if those legs were handled outside the Artifact as informal operations, the specification would describe only the on-chain half of the balance sheet while the counterparty risk sat undocumented.

The honest reading is that Spark's Liquidity Layer is a hybrid system. It carries smart contract risk from DeFi venues and institutional counterparty risk from Paxos, Anchorage and Binance simultaneously, and the Atlas's contribution is to make the second kind as explicitly configured as the first rather than to avoid it.
description: Paxos conversions, Anchorage custody and named Binance transfer legs each get their own Instance Configuration Document, pulling off-chain counterparties inside the Artifact's specification.
